title: Day Night Map: The Live Terminator Line
description: Watch the live boundary between daylight and darkness sweep the world on the Day Night Map — terminator, subsolar point and local Sun times. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, at the June solstice the terminator tilts so far that the whole Arctic sits in daylight while the Antarctic cap stays dark — the map's tilt is the season, drawn live.
quick_answer: The Day Night Map shows the live boundary between day and night across the world — the terminator — with the subsolar point where the Sun stands directly overhead. Watch the night hemisphere move, and click any point for its sunrise and sunset: the planet's clockwork, drawn as one picture.
steps_intro: One line divides breakfast from bedtime on Earth right now:

body.t: Before ringing Sydney from Chicago, look at the map: the terminator tells you whether it is 3 p.m. or 3 a.m. there more honestly than mental timezone arithmetic. The
Radio propagation and satellite passes ride the terminator. Operators have watched this line for a century because dawn and dusk change what the sky carries.
Freeze the map at a solstice and the tilt explains everything textbooks diagram badly — why hemispheres take turns, and why the poles get their six-month days.
Chasing a sunset landing or a night arrival? The map shows the darkness front your flight is racing, at the speed the terminator actually moves.

At the equator the line sweeps westward at about 1,670 km/h (the Earth's rotation: 40,075 km of circumference in 24 hours). Your sunset is that line arriving at the speed of a fighter jet — and leaving just as fast.

popular_table.note: The map is computed from the Sun's position for the current instant (or the moment you set) — geometry, not a satellite photograph. Clouds are having their own day regardless.

faq: Where is the subsolar point right now?
Over the spot where the Sun is at its highest — its latitude equals the Sun's declination for the date (up to ±23.44°) and its longitude is wherever local solar noon is happening this minute.
How often does the picture change?
Continuously in principle — the terminator moves about 15° of longitude per hour. The map refreshes on its live cycle; a minute's patience shows real motion near the line.
Can I check a future date?
The terminator belongs to an instant. Day-length and twilight tools answer date questions; this map's gift is the present tense, plus the intuition it builds.
Why does the night edge look soft in real life?
The map draws the geometric line; the sky grades through twilight bands on both sides of it — civil, nautical, astronomical — each computed by this site's twilight calculators.
Is the southern summer really the mirror?

Yes and slightly no: seasons mirror, but Earth's elliptical orbit makes southern summers a touch shorter and sharper (perihelion falls in January). The map shows the geometry; the orbit supplies the footnote.
What is the grey line in radio terms?
Amateur radio's 'gray line' is this same terminator band — signals along it travel unusually far at dawn and dusk. The map on this page is the one operators picture.
Does the map show the Moon's night too?
The terminator here is the Sun's. The Moon Position Map draws the lunar counterpart — where the Moon is up, and how lit it looks.
